title: C0: Building and testing the detectors that look for hidden bits
summary_plain: Before looking at Dolos we wrote small programs, called detectors, that spot the tiny choices a secret-message writer would use, such as British or American spelling, a swapped synonym, a split sentence or an odd word count; on text where we planted the hidden bits ourselves they found every planted change and never reported a change in untouched text.
hypothesis: Preparation, not a test of Dolos: if Dolos hides bits the StegoBench way, the bits sit in a known list of small choices, so detectors for those choices must be exact before we use them.
method_steps: Read the StegoBench dataset card and the original papers; write one description per scheme (schemes.md).
Write 11 detectors, each comparing an input sentence with its rewrite and listing the small choices the rewrite made; a choice counts only if the output has more of it than the input.
Run the Fake Encoder's four hide-and-read rules on its 500 rewrites, with its stored bits and with fresh random bits, and check the bits come back.
Run each detector on the Fake Encoder's before-and-after pairs and compare with the slots it actually changed.
Run every detector on 6,500 untouched texts (the same text as input and output); it must report nothing.

positive.what: the Fake Encoder's text with known hidden bits (8 sets of 500 rewrites)
positive.pass_number: round trip 100%, detector misses and false alarms both 0

negative.what: untouched text: 6,500 texts given to 11 detectors as their own rewrite

criteria.text: Round trip 100% on the Fake Encoder's 500 sentences for all four schemes
Detectors report no edits on untouched text

what_this_tells_us: Our detectors are exact on rule-based hidden bits of the four kinds the Fake Encoder plants, and they stay silent on unchanged text. That makes them a sound ruler for the later experiments that count Dolos's choices. Reading the StegoBench dataset card also gave the hunt its most useful clue: the training prompt was raw text, '<secret>bits</secret> sentence' followed by 'Output:', with no chat template. That is why the next experiments test this raw format next to ordinary chat prompts.
limitations: The detectors for which/that, contractions and the Oxford comma are simple text patterns, not grammar parsers.
The write-ups of the generative StegoBench schemes come from the original papers as we remember them, because the StegoBench data itself is gated.
The synonym table is a small, cautious subset of WordNet; real synonym schemes use many more pairs.

steps.what_happens: 20 rows per corpus, a few seconds
full validation, ~20 s on CPU, writes results/run_*/

flow.stage: Fake Encoder text (8 x 500) and 6,500 untouched texts

background: Dolos is a fine-tuned copy of the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct model (Dolos for short, and Qwen for the original). Earlier work on its weights showed that the fine-tune changed exactly the parts of the model that decide small writing choices: a full stop versus a comma, 'which' versus 'that', British versus American spelling, curly versus straight quotes. Poseidon Research, who released Dolos, also published StegoBench, a benchmark that trains Qwen models to hide secret bits in such choices while rewriting sentences. So the leading idea of the hunt is that Dolos hides a message (bits) inside the small choices of a rewritten text, like a spy writing a normal-looking letter (hypothesis H1).

To test that idea we first need instruments. This step, C0 (Codebreakers' preparation step), does two things. It writes down the rules of every StegoBench scheme from public material, and it builds detectors: programs that compare an input sentence with its rewrite and list every small choice the rewrite made. Each kind of choice that could hide a bit is called a carrier.

A positive result here means the detectors are trustworthy, so later experiments can count Dolos's choices with them. A negative result would mean every later count is suspect. This step says nothing about Dolos itself.

metrics.name: Round-trip success
metrics.what_it_is: The Fake Encoder (our rule-based program that hides bits in spelling, synonyms, sentence breaks or word count; code M3) hides a bit string in a sentence, its decoder reads it back, and we check the bits match.
metrics.how_to_read: 100% means the hiding rules are self-consistent; anything less means the encoder or decoder is buggy.
metrics.why_this_one: Every later control uses the Fake Encoder's text as ground truth, so its own rules must be exact.
metrics.threshold: 100% on all 500 sentences for each of the 4 schemes and both bit patterns.
metrics.threshold_why: These are deterministic rules; a single failure is a bug, not noise.

metrics.name: Detector misses and false alarms on planted text
metrics.what_it_is: For each Fake Encoder sentence we know which slots were changed; we count changes the detector missed and changes it reported that were never made.
metrics.how_to_read: Zero and zero means the detector sees exactly the planted edits.
metrics.why_this_one: It is the most direct test of whether a detector measures what it claims.
metrics.threshold: 0 misses and 0 false alarms; the detected change rate within 1 point of the planted rate (the later rewrite test, C1, allows 5).
metrics.threshold_why: The detectors are rules too, so we demanded exactness here and kept the looser 5-point bar for later use on real model text.

metrics.name: Edits reported on untouched text
metrics.what_it_is: We give each detector the same sentence as input and output.
metrics.how_to_read: Any reported edit is a false alarm by definition.
metrics.why_this_one: If a detector fires on identical text it would inflate every count later.
metrics.threshold_why: An identical pair has no choices to report.

controls_plain: The positive control is the Fake Encoder's text, where we planted the hidden bits ourselves: the detectors found all of them (for example 29 of 29 spelling changes and 249 of 249 word-count changes) and invented none. The negative control is untouched text: 6,500 sentences given to all 11 detectors as their own rewrite produced 0 reported edits. One earlier run missed 3 synonym changes because the detector ignored capital letters ('phone' versus 'Phone'); we fixed that and the rerun is the headline.

table_row.Measure: Round trip, 4 schemes x 2 bit patterns

results_plain.sentence: The Fake Encoder's four schemes, UK-versus-US spelling (shirali), synonym swap (chang_clark), sentence split and word-count parity (length parity), hide and recover bits perfectly on all 500 sentences, which meets the 100% bar.

table_row.Result: all found (e.g. spelling 29 of 29); 0 false alarms

results_plain.sentence: On text with planted bits, every detector reports exactly the planted changes, so the detected rate equals the planted rate (for example 53.7% detected versus 53.7% planted for spelling), well inside the 1-point bar.
No detector ever reports a change when the text did not change, which meets the zero bar.
Every StegoBench scheme has a one-paragraph description of what carries the bit and what 0 and 1 look like, marked by whether the source is the dataset card, the original paper, or our own guess.

fluke_check.repeats: One run of fixed rules over 500 sentences per set (8 sets) and 6,500 untouched texts; a rerun gives identical counts.
fluke_check.chance_level: There is no chance level: a rule either matches the planted edits or it does not.
fluke_check.p_value: No p-value is needed, because nothing random is involved.
fluke_check.seed_spread: The only random part, the fresh test bits, used seed 7; any other seed gives 100% round trips too, because the rules are exact.

tells_us: Our detectors are exact on rule-based hidden bits of the four kinds the Fake Encoder plants, and they stay silent on unchanged text. That makes them a sound ruler for the later experiments that count Dolos's choices. Reading the StegoBench dataset card also gave the hunt its most useful clue: the training prompt was raw text, '<secret>bits</secret> sentence' followed by 'Output:', with no chat template. That is why the next experiments test this raw format next to ordinary chat prompts.
does_not_tell_us: It tells us nothing about Dolos; no model was run. The detectors only know fixed word tables (847 spelling pairs, 141 synonym pairs), so a scheme with a different word list, or one that hides bits in which exact words a language model samples, would slip past them. Later experiments add tests that need no word list for that reason.

inspect.what_you_will_see: All 4,000 Fake Encoder sentences used in the check: the original rewrite, the version with hidden bits, the true bits, how many slots were changed, how many changes the detector found, and whether they match. Filter by scheme and by random or fixed bits.

raw_files.what: every sentence with its planted bits and the detector's findings
